title: Random variables, the binomial and the normal model
summary: Expected value, the binomial model for counts, z-scores and the 68-95-99.7 rule.
bookRef: ITILA ch. 2 (§2.1 probabilities and ensembles), ch. 23 (Useful Probability Distributions)
objectives: Compute the expected value (and SD) of a discrete random variable.
Check the four binomial conditions and compute binomial probabilities, mean and SD.
Standardise a value with a z-score to compare across scales.
Use the 68-95-99.7 rule to estimate normal probabilities.

warmup.prompt: **Predict.** A lottery ticket costs €2. It pays €100 with probability 1/100 and nothing otherwise. Over many tickets, what do you gain on average per ticket?
warmup.explain: On average a ticket returns $100 \times 0.01 = €1$, and you paid €2, so you lose €1 per ticket in the long run. That long-run average is the **expected value** - this session's first idea.

blocks.md:
## Random variables and expected value
A **random variable** $X$ assigns a number to each outcome of a random process: the prize of a lottery ticket, the number of heads in 10 flips. Its **probability distribution** lists the possible values and their probabilities (which add to 1).

The **expected value** is the long-run average of $X$:
$$E(X) = \mu = \sum x \, P(X = x)$$
and the variance measures spread around it:
$$\operatorname{Var}(X) = \sigma^2 = \sum (x - \mu)^2 \, P(X = x), \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}$$

blocks.title: A fair die
steps: $E(X) = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 3.5$ - a value you can never roll, yet the long-run average.
Squared deviations from 3.5: $6.25, 2.25, 0.25, 0.25, 2.25, 6.25$; their average is $17.5/6 = 2.917$.

reflect.prompt: Why can an expected value be a number the variable never takes?
reflect.answer: It is an average over many repetitions, not a prediction for a single outcome - just as an average family can have 1.6 children.

blocks.title: Exactly 3 heads in 5 flips
steps: One particular order, such as HHHTT, has probability $0.5^3 \times 0.5^2 = 1/32$.

blocks.md: **Predict:** with $n = 10$ and $p = 0.3$, which count is most likely? What happens to the shape as $n$ grows to 60? Check your guess.

## The normal model and z-scores
Many measurements - heights, measurement errors, averages of many values - follow a bell-shaped **normal distribution** $N(\mu, \sigma)$: symmetric around the mean $\mu$, with spread set by $\sigma$.

A **z-score** says how many SDs a value lies from the mean:
$$z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$
z-scores put different scales on one ruler. For any normal distribution:

| Within | of the mean | holds about |
|---|---|---|
| 1 SD | $\mu \pm \sigma$ | 68% |
| 2 SD | $\mu \pm 2\sigma$ | 95% |
| 3 SD | $\mu \pm 3\sigma$ | 99.7% |

blocks.title: Which result is more impressive?
steps: Ana scores 650 on test A (mean 500, SD 100). Ben scores 25 on test B (mean 20, SD 4).
Ana's result is further above her test's mean, measured in SDs: relatively more impressive.

blocks.md: **Predict:** what share of values fall below $\mu + 1\sigma$? (Hint: 68% are within one SD, split symmetrically.) Set the cut-off one SD above the mean and check.
The normal model is an **approximation**. Before you use it, look at a histogram: strongly skewed data (incomes, waiting times) are not normal, and the 68-95-99.7 rule will mislead you there.

quiz.prompt: Which situation fits the binomial model?
options: The number of heads in 20 flips of a coin
The number of flips until the first head
The number of red cards among 5 cards dealt from a 10-card pile
quiz.explain: Coin flips are binary, independent, fixed in number and share the same $p$.
feedback: The number of trials is not fixed in advance (that is the geometric distribution).
Heights are measurements, not success/failure counts.
Dealing without replacement from a small pile changes $p$ after every card, so trials are not independent.

quiz.prompt: Exam scores are approximately $N(70, 10)$. Which score is more unusual: 95 or 50?
quiz.explain: $z_{95} = (95 - 70)/10 = 2.5$ and $z_{50} = (50 - 70)/10 = -2$. The score 95 lies further from the mean in SD units.

cards.front: Expected value of a discrete random variable?
cards.back: $E(X) = \sum x\,P(X = x)$: the probability-weighted average, i.e. the long-run mean.
Binary outcomes, Independent trials, fixed Number of trials $n$, Same success probability $p$.

cards.front: Mean and SD of a binomial count?

cards.back: $z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$: how many SDs $x$ lies above (+) or below (−) the mean.
For a normal distribution about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 SDs of the mean.

cards.front: About what share of a normal distribution lies more than 2 SDs above the mean?
cards.back: About 2.5%: 95% lies within 2 SDs, so 5% lies outside, half in each tail.
